pages.label: HVAC
pages.title: Text back every missed call automatically for an HVAC business
pages.summary: When a call is missed during a job, send an automatic text asking for the address and issue, log the reply, and alert the on-call tech.
steps: Connect your business phone system (a VoIP service such as OpenPhone, Dialpad or a Twilio number) so it fires a webhook or Zapier trigger on missed calls.
In Zapier, Make or n8n, send an SMS: “Sorry we missed you — this is {Company}. Reply with your address and the issue (no heat / no cool / maintenance) and we'll call back within the hour.”
Log every reply to your CRM or a Google Sheet.
Forward the reply to the on-call technician's phone.

p: Tools: Phone system webhook → Zapier/Make/n8n → SMS → Sheet/CRM. Costs: see each vendor's current pricing page.
SMS consent rules (TCPA and 10DLC registration in the US): only text numbers that called you, include your business name, and honor STOP.

pages.label: Service businesses
pages.title: AI virtual receptionist that answers FAQs and books on Google Calendar
pages.summary: Use an AI receptionist to answer common questions from a business-info sheet, check Google Calendar availability, book appointments, and log every conversation to Sheets.
steps: Write a short business-info sheet: hours, services, pricing ranges you approve, location, parking, and FAQs you want answered without a human.
Connect Google Calendar (the booking calendar) and a Google Sheet for conversation logs.
In n8n (or similar), wire an AI agent that reads the info sheet, checks free slots on Calendar, creates events when the caller confirms, and appends a row to Sheets.
Add a clear handoff: if the question is outside the sheet, or the caller asks for a human, route to your phone or email.
Test with a few sample chats before pointing real callers at it.

p: Tools: n8n + Google Calendar + Google Sheets + an AI model. A public n8n template covers an AI-powered virtual receptionist with Calendar booking and Sheets logging: https://n8n.io/workflows/8326-create-an-ai-powered-virtual-receptionist-with-google-calendar-and-sheets/

Don't invent prices or policies in the AI answers — only allow what is on your approved info sheet.
If you add SMS or WhatsApp, follow TCPA and carrier rules: identify the business, honor STOP, and only message people who opted in or who contacted you first.
Keep a human handoff for edge cases, complaints, and anything medical, legal or financial.

pages.label: Retail
pages.title: Alert staff when a SKU drops below your reorder threshold
pages.summary: Watch an inventory sheet or POS export; when a SKU falls below the threshold you set, alert staff and optionally draft a supplier reorder email for approval.
steps: Keep live stock counts in a Google Sheet (or export SKUs nightly from your POS into one).
Add a reorder_threshold column per SKU and a supplier email column if you want drafted emails.
In n8n, Zapier or Make, schedule a check that finds rows where quantity is at or below the threshold.
Send a Slack/email alert to staff with SKU, quantity, and threshold.
Optionally draft a supplier email (do not auto-send until a human approves) listing items to reorder.

p: Tools: Google Sheets or POS export + n8n/Zapier/Make + email or Slack. Inventory-below-threshold alerts are a common small-business automation pattern (see https://useomniai.com/n8n-automation-ideas-small-business/).

This is different from a restaurant inventory-variance alert (usage vs sales). Here you only care that on-hand quantity crossed a reorder line.
Don't auto-order from suppliers without a human check — bad counts create bad POs.
Tune thresholds after a week or two so you aren't flooded with false alerts.

pages.label: Any local business
pages.title: Ask every customer for a Google review automatically (without review gating)
pages.summary: When a job or visit is marked complete, send every customer the same short review request with your Google review link, plus one reminder. Ask everyone, not just happy customers, and never offer a reward for the review.
steps: Get your review link from your Google Business Profile (the "Ask for reviews" or share-review-form option).
Trigger on a completed job, paid invoice or finished appointment in your booking, POS or field-service app via Zapier, Make or n8n.
Wait a few hours (or until the next morning), then text or email one short message with the link. Use the same message for every customer.
If there's no review after 3–5 days, send one reminder, then stop.
Log who was asked and when in a Google Sheet so nobody gets asked twice for the same visit.
Pair this with the review-reply recipe so every new review gets a timely, approved response.

p: Tools: your booking/POS/field app + Zapier/Make/n8n + SMS or email + a Google Sheet. Costs: see each vendor's current pricing page.

ul: Don't filter who gets asked. Google's policy says merchants may not "discourage or prohibit negative reviews, or selectively solicit positive reviews from customers". A "Did you love us? Yes → Google, No → private form" flow is exactly that.
No incentives. Google prohibits offering payment, discounts or free goods or services in exchange for a review, and the FTC's rule bans incentives conditioned on a positive review.

pages.summary: Send a booking confirmation, then reminders about 48–72 hours out, 24 hours out (with confirm/reschedule), and a short same-day logistics text. Keep SMS to date, time and clinic name—no diagnoses—and use a vendor that will sign a BAA.

Build a layered cadence keyed to the live schedule: immediate booking confirmation (date, time, location or telehealth link, how to reschedule); a 48–72 hour reminder; a 24-hour two-way confirm/reschedule text; a short same-day logistics text 2–4 hours before.

Stop the sequence when the visit is cancelled, rescheduled or completed. Sync status from the schedule before every send so you never remind for a dead slot.
After a no-show, send one polite rebook link and create a staff task—no blame language. Review no-show and confirmation rates monthly.

pages.summary: When a shopper who already opted into SMS leaves items in cart, send one reminder within 48 hours with a link back to checkout. Use double opt-in, disclose cart reminders in your signup terms, and never collect payment by text.

Do not complete the purchase by text, collect card data by SMS, or accept a keyword as payment approval—the customer must pay on your site.
Log consent, send time and STOP replies. Keep sends inside quiet hours for the shopper's time zone, and stop if they opt out.

p: Tools: your ecommerce cart (Shopify, WooCommerce, etc.) + an SMS platform that supports double opt-in and abandoned-cart flows, or Zapier/Make/n8n as a bridge. Costs: see each vendor's current pricing page.

ul: Abandoned-cart texts are marketing under the TCPA when sent with autodialers—get prior express written consent, keep records, and honor STOP in any reasonable wording.
US carriers commonly require double opt-in, one SMS per abandoned-cart event, and send within 48 hours for this use case.
Disclose cart reminders in the signup CTA/terms and explain cart tracking in the privacy policy.
Don't text people who only browsed or who never opted into SMS. Don't stack email + three SMS nudges for the same cart if your SMS flow already used its one allowed message.
This is compliance hygiene, not legal advice—confirm current carrier and state rules with your counsel or SMS vendor.

pages.title: Check your email setup before holiday promos go out
pages.seoTitle: Holiday email check: SPF, DKIM, DMARC and unsubscribe
pages.summary: Before you send holiday promotions, make sure your domain is authenticated (SPF or DKIM at minimum, ideally SPF, DKIM and DMARC) and that marketing emails have an easy unsubscribe. Gmail requires this for senders, and unauthenticated mail may go to spam or be rejected, so it's a 30-minute check that protects your best sales weeks.

p: Your holiday offers reach the inbox instead of spam, and it gets harder for scammers to send email that pretends to be you.

ul: Google's sender guidelines say everyone sending to personal Gmail accounts must set up SPF or DKIM, and Google recommends always setting up SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

If you send more than 5,000 messages a day to Gmail accounts, SPF, DKIM and DMARC are all required, and marketing messages must support one-click unsubscribe and show a clear unsubscribe link in the body.
Google says messages that aren't authenticated this way might be marked as spam or rejected.
Google asks senders to keep the spam rate shown in Postmaster Tools below 0.10% and never let it reach 0.30%.

ol: List every tool that sends email as your domain: your mailbox (Google Workspace or Microsoft 365), your newsletter tool, and any booking, invoicing or website-form app.
In each tool, find its domain authentication setting and add the DNS records it gives you at your domain host. Your SPF record should include every service that sends for you.
Add a DMARC record. Google says the policy can start at "none". Turn on DMARC reports so you can see who sends mail using your domain.
Send a test email to a Gmail address, open it, and choose More, then Show original. Check that SPF, DKIM and DMARC say PASS.
Open one of your marketing emails and confirm there's a visible unsubscribe link. Ask your email tool whether it adds one-click unsubscribe headers (most marketing tools handle this for you).
Sign up for Google Postmaster Tools to watch your spam rate through the season.

ul: Back up your current DNS records before you change anything. A wrong SPF or DKIM edit can stop your everyday email from arriving.
Only email people who signed up. Google's guidelines say not to buy email lists or send to people who didn't sign up.
This covers deliverability, not the law. US commercial email also has to follow the FTC's CAN-SPAM rules.

p: Google: Email sender guidelines (Gmail Help) — https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126

In Zapier, Make or n8n, send each row a short email with your online booking link or phone number. Send a text only to customers who opted in to texts from you.
Optional AI step: have it write a one-line personal opener from the sheet only (for example their equipment type and the month of their last visit). Don't let it invent prices, discounts or promises.
When a customer books (your booking app's "new appointment" trigger, or staff marking the row), set the status to booked so they get no more reminders.
Send one follow-up about 7 days later to anyone who hasn't booked, then stop.
Time it to the clock change if you like: ENERGY STAR suggests planning check-ups around the spring and fall time changes, and clocks fall back on Sunday, November 1, 2026.

p: Tools: your customer list (from your field-service or invoicing software), Google Sheets, Zapier/Make/n8n, your email tool, and optionally a texting tool and an AI step. Costs: see each vendor's current pricing page.

ENERGY STAR recommends annual pre-season check-ups by a contractor. It notes contractors get busy once summer and winter arrive, so it suggests checking cooling systems in the spring and heating systems in the fall.

blocks.h: What to put in the email (from ENERGY STAR's checklist)
ul: A heating check-up should look at gas (or oil) connections, gas pressure, burner combustion and the heat exchanger.
A typical check-up also covers thermostat settings, electrical connections, lubricating moving parts, the condensate drain, and making sure the system starts, runs and shuts off properly.
Remind homeowners that ENERGY STAR says to inspect, clean or change air filters once a month, and offer to show them how.
Commercial email has to follow the FTC's CAN-SPAM rules, including a working way to opt out and your physical address.
Texts need the customer's consent. If you're not sure you have it, use email only and ask your texting provider about the rules (see the abandoned-cart SMS recipe for how consent works in practice).
Send only what the email needs to the AI step: first name, equipment type and visit month. Never addresses, payment details or notes about the home.
Don't promise safety or savings outcomes in the message. Describe what the visit checks.

pages.label: Any local business
pages.title: Get ready for Google's automated calls asking your prices and booking times
pages.seoTitle: Google's automated calls to your business: prepare or opt out
pages.summary: Google can phone your business on a customer's behalf to book an appointment, check a restaurant wait time, or confirm prices and availability. Decide in your Business Profile settings whether to allow these calls, keep a one-page answer sheet by the phone, log each call, and train staff to spot fake "Google" callers.
steps: Decide whether you want these calls. In your Business Profile, go to More Business Profile settings, then Advanced settings. Under "Google automated calls and text messages" you can turn Bookings and inquiries from customers, Keep your profile up to date, and Post to your profile on your behalf on or off. Your profile must be verified to change them.

If you keep them on, write a one-page answer sheet in a shared Google Doc: standard prices or price ranges you're happy to quote, how far out you're booking, your booking rules, current hours and, for restaurants, how to estimate the wait. Print it for the front desk.
Retailers: if you share your in-store product details through Google Merchant Center, Google says it will use that information and won't call you about inventory.
If you take bookings through an online booking provider, Google says it may book through that partner instead of calling, so keep its availability current.

Log every Google call: give staff a 3-field form (date, what was asked, what you answered) that an automation (Zapier, Make or n8n) adds to a sheet. Add "Google call" as a source if you already track how customers find you.
Review the log monthly. If the same question keeps coming up, add the answer to your website and Business Profile.

blocks.h: What Google says these calls are for
ul: Booking appointments with the customer's details, such as time, service type and party size.
Checking current restaurant wait times.
Confirming the price and availability of in-store products and services. If you share the details, Google sends the customer an email or text with your product details or service quote.
Checking your hours or the status of in-demand inventory.

p: Google says these customer-request calls are available in select regions and languages. In the US, it lists every state except Indiana, Louisiana, Minnesota, Montana and Nebraska. Google says the calls are monitored and recorded, that it limits repeat calls for the same information, and that it avoids calling late at night or early in the morning.

ul: Google says it will never ask for payment, credit card details or account passwords. If a caller asks for money to keep you on Google, it isn't Google. Make sure every staff member knows this.
Google says its automated calls tell you at the start that they're from Google and why they're calling.
Only quote prices you'll honor. Your answer can be sent to the customer as a quote.
To stop the calls on the spot, Google says you can say "Please stop calling my business." Even after opting out, you may still get occasional manual calls from Google to confirm your details.
Profile updates Google makes from these calls are marked Pending and can take up to 5 business days to review.

p: Google Business Profile Help: About automated calls and texts from Google to your business — https://support.google.com/business/answer/7690269
Google Business Profile Help: Help protect against fraudulent calls — https://support.google.com/business/answer/6212928

faq.q: Is it a real person?
faq.a: Google describes these as automated calls, and says they identify themselves as coming from Google at the start. In some cases Google says a call can come from a manual operator.

faq.q: Will turning them off hurt my listing?
faq.a: Google doesn't say it affects ranking. It does say that keeping information accurate and answering these requests can encourage customers to visit and buy.

pages.label: Tip · Retail shops
pages.title: Put your holiday offer in real text, not inside one big image
pages.seoTitle: Holiday promo emails: put the offer in live text, not images
pages.summary: Type your offer, end date and code as real text near the top of promo emails instead of baking them into one graphic. Outlook blocks downloaded pictures by default, Apple Mail and Gmail can show AI summaries, and screen readers can't read words inside an image.

p: More people see your deal: shoppers whose email app hides images, people skimming an AI-written preview on their phone, and customers who use a screen reader.

ul: Classic Outlook is set by default to block automatic picture downloads from the internet, and Outlook for Mac doesn't download internet pictures by default either. If your offer lives inside an image, those readers see a blank box until they click.
On iPhones with Apple Intelligence turned on, Apple Mail shows a short summary under each email in the inbox instead of the first lines of the message.
Gmail can show an AI Overview at the top of an email that sums up its key points.
Email agency Backstroke says these AI summaries work from an email's live text, so an offer that appears only inside an image can be left out of the summary.
The W3C's accessibility guidelines say to use real text instead of pictures of text, and that when an image does contain text, its alt text should repeat the same words.

ol: Open your last promo email in your email tool's preview with images turned off. Can you still tell what the offer is, when it ends and how to redeem it?
Rewrite the top of the email in real text: the offer, the end date, the code, and whether it works in store, online or both.
Keep your graphic as decoration. If it has words in it, give it alt text with the same words.
Make your main button a real text button in your email editor, not a picture of a button.
Put the offer in the subject line and preview text too.
Send a test to yourself on an iPhone and in Gmail, and check that the preview or summary mentions the offer.

ul: AI summaries can get things wrong, and you can't control what they say. Clear, short text at the top is your best bet.
Put exclusions and fine print in real text as well, so nobody misses them.
Whether people see these summaries depends on their device, settings, language and account, so don't promise customers what their inbox will show.
